t.6.58.1: Seeing Narāntaka slain, the bulls among the Nairṛtas cried out: Devāntaka and Trimūrdhan, and Mahodara, the descendant of Pulastya.
t.6.58.2: Mounted on a lordly elephant that resembled a cloud, the valiant Mahodara rushed toward the mighty son of Vālin.
t.6.58.3: Then mighty Devāntaka, burning with grief at his brother's calamity, seized a blazing iron club and rushed at Aṅgada.
t.6.58.4: Then the heroic Triśiras, mounting a chariot resplendent like the sun and yoked with excellent horses, advanced against the son of Vālin.
t.6.58.5: Assailed by those three lords of the Nairṛtas, who had crushed the pride of the gods, Aṅgada uprooted a tree with mighty branches.
t.6.58.6: The heroic Aṅgada swiftly hurled that great tree with its mighty branches at Devāntaka, as Śakra hurls a blazing thunderbolt.
t.6.58.7: Triśiras cut it to pieces with arrows like venomous serpents. Seeing the tree cut down, Aṅgada then leapt up.
t.6.58.8: Then that elephant among monkeys rained down trees and rocks; Triśirā, enraged, cut them to pieces with his sharpened arrows.
t.6.58.9: And Surāntaka shattered those trees with the tip of his iron club, while Triśiras rushed at the heroic Aṅgada with his arrows.
t.6.58.10: Charging upon Vāli's son on his elephant, the enraged Mahodara struck him in the chest with lances that resembled thunderbolts.
t.6.58.11: And Devāntaka, enraged, then approached Aṅgada and, swiftly striking him with an iron club, the impetuous one quickly withdrew.
t.6.58.12: Though attacked all at once by three of the foremost of the Nairṛtas, the mighty and supremely radiant son of Vālin did not waver.
t.6.58.13: Leaping up, he struck his great elephant violently with the palm of his hand; its two eyes fell out, and that elephant let out a loud roar.
t.6.58.14: Pulling out its tusk, the mighty son of Vālin rushed at Devāntaka and struck him with it in the battle.
t.6.58.15: With all his limbs trembling, like a tree shaken by the wind, he poured forth from his mouth blood the color of lac-juice.
t.6.58.16: Then the mighty Devāntaka of great splendour, having recovered himself with difficulty, whirled his terrible iron club and struck Aṅgada with it.
t.6.58.17: Then the son of the lord of the monkeys, struck by the iron club, fell to the ground upon his knees, yet he sprang up once again.
t.6.58.18: As the son of the lord of the monkeys came leaping up, Triśiras struck him on the forehead with three terrible arrows that were like venomous serpents.
t.6.58.19: Then, perceiving that Aṅgada was surrounded by three bull-like Nairṛta warriors, Hanūmān and Nīla too set forth.
t.6.58.20: Then Nīla hurled a mountain peak at Triśiras, and the wise son of Rāvaṇa split it apart with his sharpened arrows.
t.6.58.21: Pierced by hundreds of arrows, its rocky surface split asunder, that mountain peak fell down, scattering sparks and wreathed in flames.
t.6.58.22: Then Devāntaka, seeing the son of Māruta swelling in size, rushed at him in battle with his iron club, filled with excitement.
t.6.58.23: As he came rushing on, Hanūmān, the son of Māruta, leapt up and then struck him on the head with his fist, with the force of a thunderbolt.
t.6.58.24: His head crushed and shattered by the fist, his teeth and eyes knocked out and his tongue lolling, Devāntaka, son of the king of the Rākṣasas, fell lifeless to the earth all at once.
t.6.58.25: When that mighty chief of the rākṣasa warriors, the enemy of the gods, had been slain in battle, the enraged Trimūrdhā rained a fierce shower of sharp-pointed arrows upon the chest of Nīla.
t.6.58.26: Showered with those floods of arrows, his body pierced through, Nīla, guardian of the monkey host, then went limp in every limb, held in check by that mighty one.
t.6.58.27: Then Nīla, regaining consciousness, uprooted a mountain together with its clusters of trees; then, leaping up with exceedingly fierce speed, he struck Mahodara on the head with it.
t.6.58.28: Then Mahodara, shattered by the crashing fall of the rock and crushed together with that elephant, fell lifeless upon the surface of the earth, like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
t.6.58.29: Seeing his paternal uncle slain, Triśirās took up his bow, and, enraged, he pierced Hanūmān with sharpened arrows.
t.6.58.30: Then Hanumān, enraged, leapt up and tore apart the horses of Triśiras with his nails, as the king of beasts tears apart a lordly elephant.
t.6.58.31: Then Triśirās, the son of Rāvaṇa, taking up a spear like Antaka, Death, seizing Kālarātri, the Night of Doom, hurled it at the son of Anila.
t.6.58.33: Seeing that terrible-looking spear broken by Hanumān, the troops of monkeys, overjoyed, roared like thunderclouds.
t.6.58.32: Seizing that hurled spear as it flew unchecked, like a meteor cast across the sky, the tiger among monkeys broke it and roared.
t.6.58.34: Then Triśiras, the foremost of rākṣasas, raised his sword and, in his fury, plunged it into the chest of the lord of the vānaras.
t.6.58.35: Struck by the blow of the sword, the mighty Hanumān, son of Māruta, struck the three-headed one on the chest with the palm of his hand.
t.6.58.36: Struck by him with the palm of the hand, the mighty Triśiras, his hands and garments hanging loose, fell upon the ground, bereft of consciousness.
t.6.58.37: That great monkey, resembling a mountain, snatched away the sword of the falling one and roared, terrifying all the Nairṛtas.
t.6.58.38: Unable to bear that roar, the night-ranger leapt up, and having leapt up, he struck Hanumān with his fist.
t.6.58.39: At that blow of the fist the great monkey grew furious, and, enraged, he seized the bull among rākṣasas by his diadem.
t.6.58.40: Enraged, the son of Anila cut off his heads, adorned with crowns and earrings, with a sharp sword, just as Śakra once cut off the heads of the son of Tvaṣṭṛ.
t.6.58.41: Those heads of Indra's foe, wide-eyed and like mountains, their eyes like blazing fire, fell to the earth like stars loosed from the path of the sun.
t.6.58.42: When that enemy of the gods, Triśīrṣa, had been slain by Hanumān, whose valour equalled Śakra's, the monkeys roared, the earth shook, and the Rākṣasas fled in all directions.
t.6.58.43: Seeing Triśiras slain, and likewise Mahodara, and beholding the two invincible ones, Devāntaka and Narāntaka, slain,
t.6.58.44: The mighty Mahāpārśva, extremely intolerant of insult, became enraged, and he seized a beautiful, gleaming mace made entirely of iron.
t.6.58.45: It was bound with bands of gold and smeared with flesh and blood; it shone splendid in its form, reddened with the blood of enemies.
t.6.58.47: Seizing his mace, the mighty Mahāpārśva, enraged, charged at the monkeys, blazing like the fire at the end of an age.
t.6.58.46: Its tip blazing with fiery energy, adorned with red garlands, it struck terror into the elephants Airāvata, Mahāpadma and Sārvabhauma.
t.6.58.48: Then the mighty monkey Ṛṣabha leapt up and, approaching Mahāpārśva, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, stood before him.
t.6.58.49: Seeing that mountain-like monkey standing before him, he, enraged, struck him on the chest with a mace like a thunderbolt.
t.6.58.51: Regaining consciousness after a long while, Ṛṣabha, that bull among the monkeys, enraged and with quivering lips, glared up at Mahāpārśva.
t.6.58.50: Struck by him with that mace, that bull among monkeys, his chest shattered and his body violently shaken, streamed with much blood.
t.6.58.53: Shattered by his own mace, his teeth and eyes scattered, Mahāpārśva fell down like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
t.6.58.52: Seizing that fearsome mace and whirling it again and again, he struck down Mahāpārśva, whose host was frenzied, at the forefront of the battle.
t.6.58.54: When that brother of Rāvaṇa was slain, the army of the Nairṛtas, vast as the ocean, cast away its weapons and, intent only on saving its life, fled, like an ocean that has burst its bounds.
